entities.name: Aachen Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Aachen Cathedral (Dom zu Aachen) in western Germany is the oldest cathedral in Northern Europe and one of the finest examples of Carolingian architecture. Built by Charlemagne between 796 and 805 CE as his palatine chapel, it became the coronation site of German kings for 600 years — 30 kings and 12 queens were crowned here between 936 and 1531 — and remains a UNESCO World Heritage site and a symbol of European Christian civilization.

Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel, the octagonal core of the cathedral, was modeled on the Byzantine Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, which Charlemagne visited and admired. The emperor brought Roman columns from Ravenna and Rome to decorate it. Charlemagne's throne — a simple marble chair assembled from quarried Roman stones — stands in the gallery above the nave and was used for coronations from Otto I (936 CE) onward. Charlemagne himself was buried in the chapel after his death in 814 CE.

The cathedral grew through medieval additions: the Gothic choir hall (14th century) houses the golden Shrine of Charlemagne (1215 CE) containing his bones, making Aachen a major pilgrimage center. The cathedral treasury includes the Cross of Lothair (c. 1000 CE), the Lothar Crystal, and the Persephone Sarcophagus in which Charlemagne was originally buried. As the symbolic center of the Carolingian Empire, Aachen Cathedral represents the fusion of Roman, Byzantine, and Germanic cultural traditions that created medieval European civilization.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aachen Cathedral as Charlemagne's throne and coronation chapel was the symbolic center of the Carolingian Empire — the political entity that created medieval European civilization and the precursor of the European Union.
